entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A rare, short-lived glowing ball-shaped phenomenon seen during thunderstorms, distinct from ordinary lightning bolts. It can float, roll, hiss, explode, pass through walls or windows, and sometimes leaves scorch marks or causes shocks, but no agreed scientific explanation exists for what it actually is.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.background: A European research coordination project on the physics of lightning, bringing together roughly thirty researchers, whose proposal stated that the reality of ball lightning as a phenomenon is not in doubt even though its cause is unknown.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: A label for how ball lightning research has developed as scattered, uncoordinated efforts by individual observers and theorists rather than as one unified, cumulative scientific field.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: Germany's network of ground sensors that detects and pinpoints lightning strikes across the country, letting researchers match reported ball lightning sightings to real strokes recorded at a precise time and location.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: Austria's lightning detection network, used by the author to cross-check eyewitness ball lightning reports against the timing, location, and electrical polarity of actual recorded lightning strokes.

entries.name: positive and negative lightning strokes
entries.senseHere: Lightning flashes are classified by the electrical charge they carry to the ground, positive or negative, and by the peak electrical current they deliver; the article notes an unusually high share of positive strokes among ball lightning cases compared to lightning generally.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: A 19th-century Austrian geologist and mineralogist who was a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna. He is known for his careful written and sketched descriptions of natural phenomena.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: A German physics professor famous for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment, which demonstrated that atomic particles have quantized spin in a magnetic field. This reputation makes his detailed, calculation-backed ball lightning report especially notable.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer who worked at the Jodrell Bank Observatory before becoming a physics professor at the University of Kent. His 1963 in-flight ball lightning sighting, published in Nature, became widely cited internationally.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4,302-metre mountain in Colorado's Front Range of the Rocky Mountains, site of a 19th-century high-altitude weather observatory staffed for daily meteorological readings.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: An 18th-century Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who died in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity. He was killed by an ungrounded lightning conductor, an accident later mythologized in popular engravings as a ball-lightning strike.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A 19th-century French physician regarded as the founder of modern neurology, based at the Salpetriere Hospital in Paris, and a teacher of Sigmund Freud. He studied nervous disorders following physical trauma, including cases attributed to lightning strikes.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A temporary paralysis or loss of feeling in a limb caused by a nearby lightning or ball lightning strike, which fades after hours, as distinguished from longer-lasting nerve or psychological damage.

entries.name: triggered lightning
entries.senseHere: Lightning deliberately produced for research by launching a small rocket trailing a grounded metal wire into a thundercloud, letting scientists study the discharge's effects on different materials under controlled, repeatable conditions.

entries.name: soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: A proposed explanation that ball lightning forms when a lightning strike vaporizes minerals in soil, producing a glowing cloud of burning particles whose chemical makeup matches elements found in ground spectra.

entries.name: slitless spectroscopy
entries.senseHere: A camera technique using a diffraction grating to split captured light into its component colors without a narrow slit, letting researchers read off which chemical elements a glowing object's light contains.

entries.name: cloud-ground and cloud-cloud strokes
entries.senseHere: Lightning strokes are sorted by whether they travel between a cloud and the ground or stay entirely between clouds, a distinction used to classify which type of strike accompanied each ball lightning sighting.
